title: High Availability Is Not Resilience: Why Cloud Systems Fail When It Matters Most
gist: Alexey Golev argues that high availability (surviving expected failures) is not resilience (recovering from failures nobody modeled), using an incident in which a TLS 1.3-only upgrade made Route 53 health checks fail, sending traffic away from a healthy region for about 40 minutes. He says many multi-region setups share hidden control-plane dependencies such as AWS STS's single-region global endpoint, that organizations drift into 'performative resilience', and he recommends explicit recovery ownership, recurring drills, and ARC instead of DNS failover for critical paths.

insights.claim: High availability is about surviving expected failures with minimal interruption, whereas resilience is about recovering from conditions a system was never explicitly designed to handle, and the two are routinely conflated even in strong engineering teams.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Uptime SLAs from cloud vendors and SaaS firms understate tail-risk outage exposure.
insights.quote: High availability is about surviving expected failures with minimal interruption. Resilience, on the other hand, is about recovering from conditions the system was never explicitly designed to handle.

insights.claim: Availability gets prioritized over resilience partly because availability is measurable (uptime, failover timing, replication lag) while resilience resists measurement and meaningful recovery tests are often too expensive or risky to run.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: What cannot be measured goes underfunded, so systemic outage risk accumulates out of sight.

insights.claim: A failover path that has never been exercised is not a recovery strategy but merely an assumption.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Disaster recovery claims in vendor due diligence should be judged by drill evidence, not architecture diagrams.
insights.quote: A failover path that has never been exercised is not a recovery strategy; it is just an assumption.
insights.locator: The problem is that real incidents

insights.claim: Multi-AZ redundancy models zone-level correlated failure but not software-layer correlation such as a bad config pushed to all replicas, a poisoned cache record on every read replica, or a dependency upgrade silently breaking a contract.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Correlated software failures explain why large cloud outages spread across supposedly redundant systems.
insights.quote: When independence breaks down at that level, redundancy stops working as insurance.

insights.claim: Graceful degradation is a hypothesis rather than a guarantee until tested under realistic load, for example whether a cache absorbs or amplifies pressure when a read replica lags.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Untested degradation paths can turn partial failures into cascading outages.
insights.quote: Until exercised, graceful degradation is just a hypothesis, rather than a guarantee.

insights.claim: Recovery paths rot like any unused code path: runbooks predate current dependencies, IAM policies drift, and deployment tooling changes.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: The older a system, the less its documented DR capability can be trusted.
insights.quote: Recovery is a code path like any other; unused code paths rot.

insights.claim: Route 53 HTTPS health checks require TLS 1.2 support, so a team that moved its load balancers to TLS 1.3-only for compliance caused the CDN to mark a fully healthy region unhealthy and stop routing traffic to it.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Security and compliance upgrades can trigger availability incidents through monitoring dependencies.
insights.quote: Route 53 HTTPS health checks require the target endpoint to support TLS 1.2.

insights.claim: In the TLS incident users were rerouted thousands of kilometers away, latency spiked, the failover region scaled under unprovisioned load, and the issue took roughly forty minutes to isolate because it was in the control plane, not the data plane.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Control-plane faults are slow to diagnose because internal dashboards stay green.
insights.quote: The system was highly available, but it was not resilient.

insights.claim: Afterwards it emerged that the CDN had been silently failing health checks for a week on the first batch of upgraded load balancers, and neither the regional traffic shift nor the load balancers dropping to zero traffic triggered any alert.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Alerting tuned to errors misses absence-of-traffic failures, a common blind spot in observability stacks.
insights.quote: It also emerged that the CDN had been silently failing health checks for a week

insights.claim: Monitoring that gates traffic, such as CDN health checks, is effectively part of the data path even though it lives in the control plane, and it is invisible in normal operation.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Monitoring and traffic-management vendors are a concentrated, underappreciated systemic risk.
insights.quote: monitoring that gates traffic is part of the data path, even though it lives in the control plane

insights.claim: The AWS STS global endpoint sts.amazonaws.com is hosted in a single region, US East (N. Virginia), with no automatic failover, illustrating how ostensibly global services carry hidden regional dependencies.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: us-east-1 remains a single point of failure for many 'multi-region' workloads, concentrating AWS outage risk.
insights.quote: hosted in a single AWS Region, US East (N. Virginia). Like other endpoints, it doesn't provide automatic failover to endpoints in other Regions

insights.claim: Many multi-region architectures are multi-region only in the data plane, with recovery assumptions collapsing onto a few shared control-plane dependencies such as DNS health checks, identity and routing.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Multi-region spending may buy less outage protection than buyers believe.
insights.quote: Many multi-region architectures are only multi-region in the data plane.

insights.claim: Cloud data planes are designed to keep working when control planes are impaired (EC2 instances keep running, in-flight Lambda invocations complete), but DNS-based failover built on control-plane health checks inherits control-plane failure modes.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Failover tooling choice determines whether a cloud provider incident becomes a customer outage.
insights.quote: Your failover only works if the system that decides to fail over is itself working.
insights.locator: There is a reason for this

insights.claim: Organizations usually have clear availability ownership (on-call, SLOs, escalation) but no named recovery owner, testing cadence or runbook upkeep process, a gap that exists by default rather than by decision.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Operational maturity, not architecture, is the differentiator in outage recovery.
insights.quote: Recovery ownership is often ambiguous even when uptime ownership is not.

insights.claim: Because proving recovery costs real money, carries real risk, and pays off only at the worst moment, organizations drift toward performative resilience, where standby regions and runbooks exist but recovery is assumed rather than demonstrated.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Reported DR posture across the industry likely overstates actual recovery capability.
insights.quote: Actual recovery capability is assumed rather than demonstrated
insights.locator: Part of what keeps that gap

insights.claim: The first thirty minutes of a major incident are often lost to 'dependency archaeology': drifted permissions, runbooks referencing retired tooling, and uncertainty about who understands the standby environment.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Recovery time is dominated by organizational decay, which adds directly to outage costs.
insights.quote: the first thirty minutes of a major incident are often lost to dependency archaeology

insights.claim: Recovery ownership should be separate from on-call, since on-call is about response while recovery ownership is about preparing and maintaining procedures and tooling.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Suggests a new SRE role and budget line, and a market for resilience-testing tooling.
insights.quote: Conflate the two and you get great incident commanders and runbooks that haven't been opened in eighteen months.

insights.claim: Teams that recover well run failover drills as a recurring commitment, starting small with one service and one AZ shift, and every exercise finds something broken such as a revoked permission, stale runbook or silent alarm.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Supports demand for chaos engineering and deterministic simulation testing vendors.

insights.claim: A five-question recovery check: what fails first (control-plane dependencies), what the team would actually observe, whether the recovery path can be executed, who owns recovery, and what changed after the last test.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: A practical diligence checklist for judging the operational resilience of cloud-dependent businesses.

insights.claim: DNS-based failover via Route 53 is cheap and well understood but bounded to minutes by health-check intervals, propagation and client TTL caching, making it unacceptable for second-level RTOs and exposed to health-check infrastructure failures.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Firms with strict RTOs will need paid, dedicated failover tooling, an AWS upsell opportunity.
insights.quote: If your RTO is in seconds, DNS is not an acceptable choice.

insights.claim: AWS Application Recovery Controller provides explicitly flipped routing controls with continuous readiness checks, on a cluster of five regional endpoints designed to stay operable during regional impairment, operating in seconds but adding per-cluster and per-control costs and operational overhead.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Resilience is becoming a premium paid tier in hyperscaler offerings.
insights.quote: ARC doesn't remove complexity. Instead, it relocates complexity into a more explicit and dedicated operational model.

insights.claim: The author recommends a tiered approach: ARC for a small set of customer-facing critical paths such as payments, authentication and core booking, and DNS failover for internal tools and low-traffic APIs.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Resilience spend will concentrate on revenue-critical paths, not across whole estates.

insights.claim: In sufficiently complex systems resilience is probabilistic rather than provable, so the realistic goal is improving confidence by reducing unknowns, rehearsing coordination, narrowing blast radius and shortening time from failure to detection.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Outage risk can never be eliminated, so tail-risk events at cloud-dependent firms should be priced as recurring.
insights.quote: In sufficiently complex systems, resilience is probabilistic, not provable.

insights.claim: Most organizations eventually find that the recovery procedures they never exercised are the ones that fail first, a gap invisible in the architecture until the path is actually used.
insights.speaker: Alexey Golev
insights.so_what: Expect continued high-profile outages at firms with apparently redundant architectures.
insights.quote: Most organizations eventually discover that the recovery procedures they never exercised are the ones that fail first.
